characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: JSM-7800 F SEM, scanning step size 1 μm, data analysed with HKL Channel 5 software
characterization_methods.key_findings: The 10Al steel field is almost entirely ferrite (blue, α) with only a few isolated small austenite regions (red, γ); microstructure with quasi-equiaxed grains obtained under the solution treatment conditions.
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine the phase distribution and grain morphology of the 10Al steel
characterization_methods.technique: Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) phase mapping in SEM

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: TEMs operated at 200 kV (FEI-Tecnai G2 F20 and FEI Talos F200X)
characterization_methods.key_findings: [110]α // [110]DO3 SADPs show distinct 1-11_DO3, 002_DO3 and 001_B2 superlattice spots; DO3 dark-field images acquired from the {111} and {002}DO3 reflections indicate DO3 domains coexist within both B2 domains and the ferrite matrix; maximum DO3 ordered domain size approximately 19 nm in 10Al; acicular 18R martensite observed within the ferrite grains.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: as-solution-treated samples; two-beam diffraction near the [111] zone axis for dislocation analysis
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify ordered structures, DO3/B2 superlattice reflections and dislocation types in the 10Al steel
characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy: bright-field/dark-field imaging and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED)

characterization_methods.key_findings: The mass fraction of ferrite is 98.1 % for the 10Al steel (1.9 % austenite); the (110)α peak dominates.
characterization_methods.purpose: Examine the phase composition and mass fractions

characterization_methods.key_findings: Measured Al matches the nominal 10 wt% level and Al partitions into the ferrite (10Al_α = 10.18 wt% Al vs 10Al_γ = 8.51 wt% Al); carbon could not be determined in the ferrite of the 10Al steel.
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine the chemical compositions of the bulk alloys and of the austenite and ferrite phases
characterization_methods.technique: Electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) and wet-chemical analysis

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: TEM EDS (Mn, C, Fe, Al maps), 200 nm scale
characterization_methods.key_findings: Mn and C are significantly enriched in the acicular precipitates while Al is depleted, identifying the precipitates as 18R martensite formed within the ferrite during quenching.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: acicular precipitates in the ferrite of the 10Al steel
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine the elemental distribution in the acicular precipitates

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: TEM bright-field, two-beam diffraction near the [111] zone axis; samples pre-deformed to 3 % engineering strain
characterization_methods.key_findings: Long straight dislocations systematically lose contrast under g = [10-1] and g = [1-10] but are visible under g = [0-11], giving b = a/2[111] by g·b = 0 analysis; the ferrite of 10Al is predominantly composed of long straight screw dislocations.
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the Burgers vector and dislocation types in the ferrite of the 10Al steel

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: HRTEM along the [100] zone axis; IFFT along (01-1) and (0-11) planes
characterization_methods.key_findings: Dislocations are composed of a multitude of dislocation dipoles, and the DO3 superlattice is sheared along the dislocation line and slip plane by these dipoles.
characterization_methods.purpose: Reveal the interaction between dislocations and the DO3 ordered structure
characterization_methods.technique: High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) and inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT)

analytical_models.equation_role: Estimate the size D of the superlattice ordered domains from the number N of paired dislocations and the magnitude b of the Burgers vector
analytical_models.model_note: Eq. (4); applied to the 10Al steel the number of dislocation pairs usually does not exceed 6 pairs; with a paired dislocation count of 12 the ordered domain size is estimated as 3.0 nm.

computational_details.simulation_method: Analytical estimate of superlattice ordered domain size from the number of paired dislocations
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: The calculated DO3 ordered domain size in the ferrite of the 10Al steel (3.0 nm) is significantly smaller than the TEM-observed value of 19 nm, whereas the calculated size for the 8Al steel (1.5 nm) is very close to its TEM-observed value of 2.1 nm.

analytical_models.equation_role: Calculate the stacking fault energy γ_SFE of the austenite, where ρ is the molar surface density along {111} planes, ΔG^{γ→ε} is the molar Gibbs energy of the γ→ε transformation and σ is the γ/ε interfacial energy per unit area
analytical_models.model_note: Eq. (3); the calculation is described for the investigated steels but no value is tabulated for the 10Al_γ austenite.

computational_details.potential_model_or_database: Thermodynamic functions and parameters listed in literature [35]
computational_details.simulation_method: Thermodynamic calculation of the stacking fault energy of austenite
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: No γ_SFE value is reported for the 10Al_γ austenite (Table 2 gives a dash); the calculation is only documented for 4Al_γ (51.25), 6Al_γ (62.64) and 8Al_γ (68.47) mJ·m⁻².

defect_interactions.interaction_type: dislocation pairing / shearing of DO3 ordered domains (anti-phase boundary, APB, based)
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: In the 10Al steel, dislocation pairing is extremely pronounced, with up to six dislocation pairs observed and dislocation spacings as small as approximately 3 nm, demonstrating pronounced paired super-dislocation characteristics. The large-sized DO3 ordered domains in the 10Al steel cannot be completely sheared (Fig. 8(c)), whereas those in the 8Al steel can. The APB-induced attractive force in the ferrite of the 10Al steel is substantially stronger than that in the 8Al steel.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: dislocation–ordered structure interaction causing planar slip
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Both edge and screw dislocations in the 10Al ferrite show distinct planar slip; the interaction between dislocations and the DO3 ordered superlattice in the ferrite controls the planar dislocation pattern, with dislocations composed of a multitude of dislocation dipoles that shear the DO3 superlattice along the dislocation line and slip plane (HRTEM/IFFT of Fig. 8(g-i)).

interfaces.interface_notes: The TEM observation of the ferrite–austenite phase interface, where edge dislocations are readily activated at grain boundaries owing to high local stresses, and the statement that ~24.3 % austenite in 8Al steel acts as a soft phase, are reported for the 8Al steel (Fig. 7(j–l)) and are not established for the 10Al steel (which contains only 1.9 % austenite). They are noted here only as a caution and are not attributed to this sample.
interfaces.phase_evolution: With increasing Al content the phase constitution transitions from single-phase austenite (4Al) to austenite-matrix duplex (6Al) and then ferrite-matrix duplex structures (8Al and 10Al); at 10 %Al the steel is nearly fully ferritic. DO3 ordered domains coexist within both the B2 ordered domains and the ferrite, exhibiting progressive size enlargement with higher Al concentrations (maximum ~19 nm in 10Al).

phase_interfaces.coherence: DO3 ordered domains coexist within both the B2 ordered domains and the ferrite matrix (ordered domains within the ferritic matrix)

interfaces.slip_behavior: The ferrite dislocation structure in the 10Al steel is predominantly characterized by localized, long, straight screw dislocations with non-uniform distribution, which leads to plastic instability/brittle fracture; all dislocation types show distinct planar slip. The Burgers vector of the ferrite dislocations was determined to be a/2[111] by g·b = 0 analysis near the [111] zone axis.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: tensile ductility (total elongation) and strength–ductility balance

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots with nominal compositions Fe-35Mn-xAl-1C-0.1Nb-0.1V-1Mo-1W (x = 4, 6, 8, 10 wt%) prepared via vacuum induction melting under a high-purity Ar atmosphere.
As-cast ingots homogenized at 1150 °C for 4 h.
Subsequently hot-forged into rods with a diameter of 16.5 mm (tensile specimens were machined from the rods with the tensile axis parallel to the rod axis).

Bars solution-treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by oil quenching to achieve a microstructure with nearly equiaxed grains; the four solution-treated steels are hereafter referred to as 4Al, 6Al, 8Al and 10Al steels.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: At least three tensile specimens tested to fracture to ensure reproducibility; tests performed on an MTS tensile machine
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: standard tensile specimens 5 mm in diameter, 25 mm in gauge length, machined from the quenched rods with the tensile axis parallel to the rod axis

strain_hardening_rate.value: strain hardening rate falls to zero within a very small strain (Fig. 3(d))

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress–strain curve (Fig. 3(a)): the 10Al (green) curve rises steeply to a high stress yet terminates at very small strain (before 0.05). True stress–true strain curve (Fig. 3(c)): the 10Al steel reaches only a short low-strain segment. Strain hardening rate (Fig. 3(d)): the 10Al green curve falls to zero within a very small strain.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Phase-specific microhardness of the as-solution-treated steels as a function of Al content
Density measured using the principle of Archimedes

structures.microstructure_counts: 2 main phases (nearly fully ferritic matrix + few isolated austenite regions); the ferrite additionally contains B2 and DO3 ordered domains and acicular 18R martensite precipitates.

defects.type: 18R martensite precipitates and DO3/B2 ordered domains (as-solution-treated state)

phases_present.morphology: ordered domains coexisting with DO3 domains within the ferrite matrix (001_B2 superlattice reflections)

ordered domains coexisting within both the B2 ordered domains and the ferrite matrix; maximum size in 10Al estimated to be approximately 19 nm (TEM), superlattice spots the most intense of the three ferrite patterns

precipitates.distribution: acicular precipitates within the ferrite grains of the 10Al steel; significantly enriched in Mn and C while Al is depleted (TEM EDS mapping)

defects.type: L12-type short-range ordered (SRO) domains / spinodal decomposition (Al and C concentration fluctuations)

microstructure_list.region: few isolated small austenite regions within the ferrite matrix

structures.overall_structure: After solution treatment (1050 °C/2 h + oil quenching) the 10Al steel is nearly a fully ferrite phase steel (98.1 % ferrite by mass, 1.9 % austenite) with quasi-equiaxed grains; the ferrite contains B2 and DO3 ordered domains and acicular 18R martensite precipitates. EBSD phase map shows the field almost entirely blue ferrite with only a few isolated small red austenite regions.

structures.microstructure_counts: ferrite with localized long straight screw dislocations; austenite with planar slip dislocation lines

defects.type: long straight screw dislocations (predominant), non-uniform/localized distribution; a small number of mixed dislocations

structures.overall_structure: After small (~3 % engineering strain) tensile deformation the 10Al ferrite contains predominantly long, straight, non-uniformly distributed screw dislocations (only a small number of long straight dislocations activated), all exhibiting planar slip; the 10Al austenite shows complex planar slip characteristics during the early deformation stage.

unmapped_findings: The room-temperature stacking fault energy γ_SFE of the 10Al_γ austenite is not reported (Table 2 lists an en-dash '–' for 10Al_γ); values are only given for 4Al_γ (51.25), 6Al_γ (62.64) and 8Al_γ (68.47) mJ·m⁻².

Measured chemical composition of the 10Al steel (wt.%): bulk 10Al — Mn 34.66, Al 10.17, C 0.097, Nb 0.11, V 0.11, Mo 1.30, W 1.38, Fe Bal.; austenite 10Al_γ — Mn 37.39, Al 8.51, C not determined (-), Nb 0.08, V 0.09, Mo 0.80, W 0.81, Fe Bal.; ferrite 10Al_α — Mn 34.13, Al 10.18, C not determined (-), Nb 0.08, V 0.11, Mo 1.24, W 1.26, Fe Bal. The table documents that Al partitions into the ferrite.

The 10Al steel after solution treatment is nearly a fully ferrite phase steel (98.1 % ferrite / 1.9 % austenite mass fractions from XRD) that exhibits brittle behaviour with only ~4.6 % total elongation.
The degradation in plasticity of the 10Al steel is attributed to the coarsening of DO3 ordered domains and the formation of 18R martensite.
The measured densities of the four investigated steels by the Archimedes principle are 7.42, 7.18, 6.99 and 6.84 g cm⁻³ for the 4Al, 6Al, 8Al and 10Al steels, respectively (10Al: 6.84 g cm⁻³).
The solution-treated alloy is designated '10Al steel' as part of the naming scheme applied to all four solution-treated steels (4Al, 6Al, 8Al and 10Al).

Table 3 column 1 is headed 'Test temperature' although its entries are the alloy labels 4Al, 6Al, 8Al and 10Al; the 10Al tensile row is 585 (±29) MPa YS, 613 (±41) MPa UTS, 2.1 (±1.1) % uniform elongation and 4.6 (±1.6) % total elongation, all measured at room temperature.
The DO3/18R-related flow-stress decomposition (Eqs. 5–8, Table 4, Fig. 9) with K = 0.75 and σ0 = 455 MPa is performed specifically for the 8Al steel and is not reported for the 10Al steel.
